episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, May 5th. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Leading off today's Innovation Pulse, seventy percent of college students view artificial intelligence as a threat to their job prospects, according to a 2025 Harvard Kennedy School poll. The poll results come as students across the country reconsider their career paths. At Miami University, Josephine Timperman switched from business analytics to marketing after realizing that basic technical skills like coding and statistical analysis can be easily automated. She now focuses on relationship-building skills that she believes A.I. cannot replicate. Ben Aybar at University of Chicago applied to roughly fifty software engineering positions and received zero interview callbacks. He is now pursuing a master's degree in computer science while doing A.I. consulting work on the side. At University of Virginia, data science major Ava Lawless is questioning her field's viability despite conflicting opinions from her advisors, and is considering switching to studio art. A separate Gallup poll found that forty-eight percent of Gen Z workers believe A.I. workforce risks outweigh the benefits. Courtney Brown of the Lumina Foundation said the concentration of students changing majors specifically because of A.I. is unusual compared to historical patterns. The same poll found fifty percent of Gen Z adults use A.I. weekly, and teenagers report even higher usage rates. Brown University President Christina Paxson emphasized that communication and analytical thought matter most for future success rather than specific technical skills like Java coding.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I. today, University of Michigan faculty voted seventeen hundred eleven in favor of creating A.I.-free zones on campus, according to The Michigan Daily. The Faculty Senate passed Motion #042726-2 requesting the university create infrastructure to detect A.I. use in student work and establish courses where students complete assignments without A.I. tools. The motion also requests a lockdown browser option to prevent A.I. access on specific assignments. Assistant law professor Salome Viljoen said that while A.I. can enhance productivity, she sees risk that A.I. poses to the cognitive conditions necessary to produce new experts. Associate history professor Carina Ray advocated for A.I.-free zones as spaces where students can have access to writing technology that allows them to think in much more elastic ways.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Investing in Innovation, students in a Moraine Valley Community College history class recently questioned a virtual George Washington in real time. Dr. John Sands said faculty created the A.I.-powered virtual guest speaker using a nearly one million dollar National Science Foundation grant. Sands directs the four-year grant program called Leveraging Artificial Intelligence Skills in Community College Classrooms and Technical Careers. Faculty from English, physical science, mathematics, career programs, and health sciences have created A.I.-generated mind maps, flowcharts, and anatomical illustrations for their courses. Faculty are also building exams and presentations using A.I. tools. The grant provides training for faculty across multiple academic disciplines on A.I. classroom integration techniques. After one year, Moraine Valley will share the training materials and resources with community colleges across the country.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Case Study, education students at University of North Georgia are using A.I. teaching methods in partner K-12 schools through the Emerging Technology Teaching Academy, which launched in fall 2025. The program places education majors in nearby county schools to practice current A.I. classroom techniques with real students. Students are practicing a specific technique in their placements: having K-12 pupils use A.I. to summarize books, then guiding them to analyze how the A.I. generalized or oversimplified the content. Student Xander Thrailkill said A.I. can be used as a tool to differentiate lessons and save time. Student Jarintzi Orozco Garcia said the program emphasizes modeling ethical and responsible A.I. use for future students.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Case Study, Princeton's physics department is comparing faculty grades with A.I.-generated grades on student exams without affecting official scores. The Daily Princetonian reported that the experiment involves PHY 104: General Physics II, a course with approximately two hundred thirty students. Professor Lyman Page said the department chose Google's Gemini Pro enterprise version to make sure this doesn't get outside of anything at Princeton. Student participation is voluntary. The experiment addresses a practical efficiency challenge: one faculty member currently grades all problems for two hundred thirty students over two days. Students raised substantive concerns. Sean Egan said he approved participation only because human faculty grade first. Tova Jean-Louis warned that A.I. can hallucinate information and reproduce biases.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Beyond Ed today, the Trump administration is preparing an executive order requiring all new A.I. models to be vetted before public release, according to CIO. The Center for A.I. Standards and Innovation, a Commerce Department division under NIST, will conduct the pre-release evaluations. CAISI has signed new agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI. The agency already had partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI from 2024. Technology analyst Carmi Levy said the order would be the first mandatory pre-release testing requirement from this administration.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

quickHits.headline: Michigan Faculty Senate Votes 1,711 to Create A.I.-Free Zones on Campus

The Faculty Senate passed Motion #042726-2 requesting the university create infrastructure to detect A.I. use in student work and establish courses where students complete assignments without A.I. tools. The motion also requests a lockdown browser option to prevent A.I. access on specific assignments. Faculty members raised concerns during the senate meeting about A.I.'s effects on student cognitive development and academic skill-building. Associate history professor Carina Ray advocated for A.I.-free zones as spaces where "students can have access to the type of writing technology that allows them to think in much more elastic ways." The motion requests the university provost report back to the senate on implementation progress.

quickHits.headline: Moraine Valley Uses $1 Million NSF Grant to Build A.I. Virtual Guest Speakers, Training Materials
quickHits.summary: Students in a Moraine Valley Community College history class recently questioned a virtual George Washington in real time. "We had George Washington come into class and the students could literally ask him questions," Dr. John Sands said. Faculty created the A.I.-powered virtual guest speaker and other educational materials using a nearly $1 million National Science Foundation grant. Sands directs the four-year grant program called "Leveraging Artificial Intelligence Skills in Community College Classrooms and Technical Careers." Faculty from English, physical science, mathematics, career programs, and health sciences have created A.I.-generated mind maps, flowcharts, and anatomical illustrations for their courses. Faculty are also building exams and presentations using A.I. tools. The grant provides training for faculty across multiple academic disciplines on A.I. classroom integration techniques. After one year, Moraine Valley will share the training materials and resources with community colleges across the country. The Illinois community college is located in Palos Hills, southwest of Chicago.

quickHits.headline: UNG Education Students Practice A.I. Teaching Methods in Partner K-12 Schools
quickHits.summary: Education students at University of North Georgia are using A.I. teaching methods in partner K-12 schools through the Emerging Technology Teaching Academy, which launched in fall 2025. The program places education majors in nearby county schools to practice current A.I. classroom techniques with real students. Dr. April Nelms, a professor of education, told UNG that faculty "worked hand in hand with our partners to make sure we were producing the type of educators they would want." Students are practicing a specific technique in their placements: having K-12 pupils use A.I. to summarize books, then guiding them to analyze how the A.I. generalized or oversimplified the content. Student Xander Thrailkill said A.I. "can be used as a tool to differentiate lessons and save time." Student Jarintzi Orozco Garcia said the program emphasizes modeling "ethical and responsible" A.I. use for future students. Student Christopher Pope said faculty acknowledge that "A.I. is not going away."

quickHits.headline: Princeton Physics Department Tests A.I. Grading on 230-Student Course
quickHits.summary: Princeton's physics department is comparing faculty grades with A.I.-generated grades on student exams — without affecting official scores. The Daily Princetonian reported that the experiment involves PHY 104: General Physics II, a course with approximately 230 students. Professor Lyman Page, the course head, said the department chose Google's Gemini Pro enterprise version "to make sure this doesn't get outside of anything at Princeton." Student participation is voluntary. The experiment addresses a practical efficiency challenge: one faculty member currently grades all problems for 230 students over two days. Page described the pilot cautiously: "It's an experiment. I think is the way to view it, and we'll just see how it goes." Students raised substantive concerns. Sean Egan '29 said he approved participation only because human faculty grade first. Tova Jean-Louis '29 warned that "A.I. can 'hallucinate' information and reproduce biases." Grace Rivas '29 noted that "A.I. may just detect the right or wrong answer" without understanding student reasoning. A university spokesperson clarified this is a department-level initiative, not an institution-wide pilot.

quickHits.headline: White House Prepares Executive Order Requiring A.I. Model Vetting Before Public Release
quickHits.summary: The Trump administration is preparing an executive order requiring all new A.I. models to be vetted before public release, CIO reported. The Center for A.I. Standards and Innovation, a Commerce Department division under NIST, will conduct the pre-release evaluations. CAISI has signed new agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI. The agency already had partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI from 2024. The administration had previously not imposed pre-release testing requirements on A.I. developers. Anthropic recently released its Mythos model, which demonstrated capability for finding network vulnerabilities. CAISI stated it will "conduct pre-deployment evaluations and targeted research to better assess frontier A.I. capabilities and advance the state of A.I. security." Technology analyst Carmi Levy said the order would be the first mandatory pre-release testing requirement from this administration. The agreements now cover five A.I. developers: Google DeepMind, Microsoft, xAI, Anthropic, and OpenAI. CAISI operates under the National Institute of Standards and Technology within the Commerce Department.
